correctness.rationale: The constructive proof reduces all per-round EF1 allocations to pairs, forces balanced counts by aggregate EF, and characterizes every unrestricted aggregate Pareto improvement as a bounded positive integer exchange with slope in the exact closed interval of value ratios. Distinct endpoints guarantee strict improvement; coincident endpoints imply none. Integer endpoint fraction and consecutive-ratio construction establish the sharp cutoff. Independently enumerated 5,292 unrestricted aggregate cases and 109,220 complete sequences corroborate the proof, not replacing its infinite scope.

originality.rationale: Igarashi et al. (arXiv:2304.01644v1) proved two-round feasibility and one fixed repeated-EF1 incompatibility witness, not the continuous-valuations full horizon criterion, exact sequence count or sharp integer cutoff. The closest repeated-matching paper imposes different feasibility and efficiency concepts. The multiset fair-division paper addresses overall EF/EFX and lacks the triple conjunction. published-finding corpus semantic searches and primary full-text inspection found no dominating statement; residual unindexed-equivalence risk remains.
residual_risks: Unindexed or inaccessible specialist work may formulate the same result as a two-commodity discrete exchange or a periodic fair scheduling lemma.

value.rationale: An exact classification of a natural local-versus-global fairness/efficiency conflict for recurring two-good assignments. The integer-exchange cutoff predicts exactly when an apparently fair schedule first becomes Pareto-dominated, counts all successful schedules, and proves sharp arbitrarily long delay from near-aligned but nonproportional positive valuations; this refines the initiating article’s single counterexample and is not an arbitrary numerical slice.
